items.source: Neil Sethi / As We Approach The Open
items.title: Trump threatens 'economic warfare on an unprecedented scale' against Iran's oil buyers (China)
items.idea: Trump posted that trade partners buying Iranian oil face isolation "on an unprecedented scale," with China as the obvious primary target since it buys the bulk of Iran's crude. Same session: a tanker hijacked in the Gulf of Aden, oil pressing 3-week highs, S&P giving back all of Wednesday's gains.
items.angle: This stacks directly on top of chip export controls as a second economic front against China -- energy this time, not just compute.
items.tweetA: Trump just threatened 'economic warfare on an unprecedented scale' against anyone buying Iranian oil. China buys most of it. Add that to chip export controls and the two fronts against China are now energy AND compute.
items.tweetB: Oil at 3-week highs, a tanker hijacked in the Gulf of Aden, and Trump threatening isolation on Iran's buyers, all in one session that also gave back the whole Wednesday equity rally. Nobody's pricing this tail risk yet.

items.source: Neil Sethi / As We Approach The Open
items.title: A fifth of global LNG flows are shut in -- European winter gas bills about to double
items.idea: About 20% of global LNG flows are shut in following the Strait of Hormuz blockade. Winter gas prices are already 2x year-earlier levels, German power is up 50%, and European gas storage is at its lowest seasonal level on record -- worsened by Asia pulling cargoes away from Europe.
items.angle: Everyone is trading the oil headline; the LNG supply chain is where the real European inflation shock is quietly building into Q4.
items.tweetA: Everyone's watching oil. The bigger story is European gas: a fifth of global LNG is shut in from Hormuz, storage is at record seasonal lows, and German power is already up 50%. Winter hasn't even started.
items.tweetB: Asia is outbidding Europe for LNG cargoes right now because Asia got hit by the Hormuz shutdown first. Europe is next in line for a shortage nobody sees until the heating season actually starts.

items.title: Japan quietly re-routed oil imports from the Mideast to the US since February
items.idea: Japan's July exports rose 23.2% y/y, the fastest since Oct 2022, on a yen at a 40-year low. Buried line: US share of Japan's oil import volume jumped from 7% in February to 36% now, while Mideast share fell to 59% from higher levels -- a real-time hedge against Hormuz risk.
items.angle: Japan is de-risking its energy supply chain months before Hormuz became the consensus trade -- a leading indicator for how other Asian importers may reposition.
items.tweetA: Japan's oil imports from the US just went from 7% to 36% of total volume since February. Nobody's writing headlines about it, but that's Japan hedging Hormuz risk with its wallet, months before Hormuz became the trade everyone's now chasing.
items.tweetB: A 40-year weak yen is doing more for Japanese exporters than any BOJ policy could. Exports +23.2% y/y, fastest since 2022. The 'weak yen hurts Japan' consensus needs an asterisk when chips and cars, not imports, are driving the number.

items.title: Foreign funds dumped the most short-dated JGBs in two decades
items.idea: Net sales of 2-5yr JGBs hit ¥1.28 trillion in July, the most since July 2006, on speculation of BOJ tightening. At the same time, foreigners still bought a net ¥889.8 billion of 10yr+ paper -- a barbell, not a wholesale bearish call.
items.angle: The curve positioning is a cleaner read on what global funds actually expect from the BOJ than any policy statement: hikes priced at the front end, safety still assumed at the long end.
items.tweetA: Foreign funds just dumped the most short JGBs in 20 years while still buying long-dated Japanese debt. That's not a bearish JGB call, it's a specific bet: hikes at the front end, long end still safe.
items.tweetB: If you want to know what smart money actually believes about BOJ policy, skip the statement and read the curve positioning: record short-end selling, continued long-end buying. That's a hike bet, not a crisis bet.

items.title: Bessent's buyback bull-flattened the curve -- and financials fell anyway
items.idea: The Treasury buyback bull-flattened the curve (2s10s 52→46bp, 2s30s 109→100bp) with the 20-year rallying 11bp. Consensus said lower yields help banks. Financials were negative on both equal-weight tapes (-0.52%/-0.39%) the same session; regional banks -2.37%. Mechanism: banks fund short, lend long -- the buyback compressed asset yields while funding costs (set by new bill issuance) stayed put, squeezing net interest margin.
items.angle: Consensus is reading this backwards -- Bessent financed a duration rescue by issuing the exact instrument that sets deposit competition, which is the worst possible curve shape for bank NIM.
items.tweetA: Bessent's buyback bull-flattened the curve and consensus said 'great for banks, lower discount rate.' Financials were red on both equal-weight tapes that day. He financed it with bills, the exact instrument that sets deposit competition. He compressed NIM to save duration.
items.tweetB: If you wanted to design one policy move to squeeze bank net interest margin, funding a long-end rally with short-end bill issuance is it. Regional banks -2.37% on a day the 20-year rallied 11bp. Read the mechanism, not the headline.

items.title: Life insurers are losing money on up days, down days, AND flat days
items.idea: Life insurance closed last of 14 subsectors for a third straight session, regardless of which way yields moved. AI-linked borrowers are now ~18% of all 2026 US IG issuance vs 1% in 2024, yielding 6-7% -- exactly the reinvestment yield general accounts reach for at 15yr+ duration, and the single-name credit has been widening for two months while the equity hasn't marked it.
items.angle: A sector that loses on every rate scenario isn't a duration story anymore -- credit may be pricing AI capex risk before equity does, and life insurers are the tell.
items.tweetA: Life insurance is down for 3 straight sessions regardless of which way rates moved. Up days, down days, flat days, doesn't matter. That's not a duration problem, that's a concentration problem: AI borrowers went from 1% to 18% of IG issuance in two years and life insurers are the natural buyer.
items.tweetB: Credit may be pricing AI capex risk before equity does. Watch life insurance stocks, not tech stocks, for the first real tell on the AI debt binge. Third straight session of losses that rates can't explain.

items.title: Robots 50x smaller than a human hair can now pick up and move a single bacterium
items.idea: Researchers in Würzburg built nanorobots roughly 50 times smaller than the width of a human hair, small enough to operate in water among cells and bacteria -- able to collect a bacterium, transport it, and release it at a chosen location.
items.angle: Genuinely novel, non-financial, and the metaphor Dauber built his entire buyback piece around (the Treasury 'shrinking itself down' inside the bond market).
items.tweetA: Robots 50x smaller than a human hair can now pick up a single bacterium, move it, and put it down. We're closer to 'Fantastic Voyage' being real than most people realize, and it happened quietly in a Würzburg lab, not a headline.
items.tweetB: The most interesting nanotech story this week has nothing to do with chips. It's robots small enough to work inside a water droplet, manipulating individual cells one at a time.

items.title: Brent spiked 2.58% -- refining equities fell anyway, and futures may not equal physical anymore
items.idea: Brent rallied 2.58% to $93.98 but refining/marketing fell -1.08%, midstream -1.21%, drilling -0.66% (crack compression, input repriced before scarcity widened the margin). Separately: Mark Leonard's Foreign Affairs piece notes that in April, Brent futures traded near $113 while physical cargoes changed hands as high as $144 -- a $31 gap on the same barrel.
items.angle: If futures and physical have come apart by $31, 'Brent settled at $93.98' is a statement about one venue, not the price of oil -- and every crack-spread model built on the screen price just got less reliable.
items.tweetA: Brent futures traded near $113 in April while physical cargoes went for as much as $144. A $31 gap on the same barrel. If the screen price and the clearing price have come apart, every refiner model built on 'Brent settled at X' just got less reliable.
items.tweetB: Oil spiked 2.58% and refining stocks fell anyway. That's not the market being wrong, that's the crack spread getting squeezed before capacity scarcity can widen it back out. Input repriced first, margin thesis intact, timing was early.

items.idea: Bridgewater's Greg Jensen and Nir Bar Dea wrote an NYT op-ed proposing a tax on companies' AI token usage (framed as machine labor's wage equivalent), estimating AI could displace 18% of current US jobs within five years, and calling for safety standards plus using tax revenue to fund government AI equity stakes. items.title: CFTC seeking comment on futures contracts tied to AI compute power
items.idea: CME Group, ICE, and Architect Financial Technologies plan to offer futures tied to AI compute cost/availability, pending CFTC approval, letting developers and data centers hedge compute the way companies hedge fuel with energy derivatives. The CFTC is specifically asking whether the market needs standardized price indexes.
items.angle: Turning compute into a hedgeable commodity is a tell that AI infra spend has crossed from a capex story into a fully financialized asset class with its own derivatives market.
items.tweetA: Compute is about to get its own futures market, same structure as energy derivatives. When an input becomes hedgeable, the market is declaring it a commodity, not a capex line item. AI infra just crossed that line.
items.tweetB: Nobody's asking the obvious question about AI compute futures: whose price index? Chip, location, and power mix all vary by data center. If the contract doesn't reflect what buyers actually use, this becomes a paper market fast.

items.tweetB: Mercor bid $7.5M as backup on a dead airline's internal data. The AI data supply chain now includes bankruptcy courts as a sourcing channel. That's a stranger sentence than anyone's making it sound.

items.title: AlphaFold worked because a 50-year dataset already existed. Cancer has no equivalent.
items.idea: Over $70B went into AI+life sciences from 2020-2024; still zero AI-discovered drugs are on the market and ~188,000 people die of cancer weekly. AlphaFold succeeded because DeepMind had a pre-built, standardized dataset (the Protein Data Bank) and a well-defined output. Cancer has no equivalent data bank -- the needed data 'has to be grown, imperfectly, at the pace of natural aging,' and biopsies kill the cells you're trying to watch evolve.
items.angle: Directly rebuts the AI-CEO cancer-cure messaging (Amodei, Altman) with a data-constraint argument that has real implications for how fast biotech-AI plays can actually pay off.
items.tweetA: $70 billion went into AI+life sciences from 2020-2024. Zero AI-discovered drugs are on the market. AlphaFold worked because a 50-year, pre-built protein dataset already existed. Cancer has no equivalent data bank, and biology can't be sped up by adding GPUs.
items.tweetB: Dario Amodei says curing cancer is now Anthropic's redemption arc. The bottleneck he's not naming: the data has to be grown at the pace of a mouse's lifespan, not a data center's clock speed. Superintelligence doesn't get around biology's calendar.

items.title: McKinsey: fertility collapse, not resource limits, is the century's defining constraint
items.idea: MGI's podcast authors argue collapsing fertility, rather than resource scarcity, may be the century's defining challenge, and that growth/adaptation can still address climate change even in an economy eight times today's size. items.angle: Thin on data but the framing is a useful mental model for any long-horizon demographic or AI-productivity debate.
items.tweetA: McKinsey's framing worth stealing: AI isn't a fixed point you hit, it's a curve you're always on. Every debate about 'has AI plateaued' assumes a finish line that was never the right model to begin with.
items.tweetB: Resource scarcity used to be the doomer's favorite constraint. McKinsey is arguing collapsing fertility is the actual binding constraint on this century's growth, a very different portfolio implication than 'peak oil' ever was.
